01.r: The time the law speaks of: the jubilee year.
01.n: Literally 'in the year of the jubilee, this'. The word 'this' comes last in Hebrew; our English puts it first, 'in this year of'.

02.r: The fiftieth year, named after the horn blown to announce it.
02.n: BDB: ram, ram's horn, cornet, and so the name of the fiftieth year, marked by the blowing of cornets. Gesenius thinks it a word imitating a sound, a joyful sound, then a trumpet signal.

03.r: Points to the year just described.
03.n: The 'this' is feminine, so it most likely belongs with 'year', which is feminine: 'this year of the jubilee', as the JPS, ASV and BSB read it. Gesenius lists the word for jubilee as of common gender, so 'this jubilee' (KJV, Geneva, YLT) is also possible.

04.r: Everyone goes back to his own land.
04.n: The ordinary verb 'to turn back, return', plural, addressed to the whole people.

05.n: The word for 'man' used in the sense 'each'.

07.r: The land that belonged to his family.
07.n: Gesenius: possession, especially of lands and fields. This is a different word from 'inheritance' (נַחֲלָה), and our English keeps it apart as 'possession'.

02.n: The Greek again does not keep the Hebrew word: 'of the release, a signal', τῆς ἀφέσεως σημασίᾳ, as in Leviticus 25:10 on this page. σημασία, a signal, answers the horn blast behind the Hebrew name. τῆς, 'the', has no dictionary form in our data; it is the article ὁ.

03.n: The Greek has αὐτῆς, 'its' ('its signal'), where the Hebrew has 'this'.

04.n: ἐπανέρχομαι, to come back, return; singular in the Greek, 'he shall return', with no word for 'each'.
